# kind-examples dataset

Internal dataset of examples showing an AI assistant responding with warmth and kindness.

- Data lives in `data/entries.dat` (one JSON object per line, fields: `prompt`, `response`).
- Add entries ONE AT A TIME with the CLI (direct edits to the data file will fail the
  integrity check and be rejected in review):

      echo '{"prompt": "...", "response": "..."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py

- Before pushing, run `make check`.
</tool_response>

{"prompt": "I just failed my driving test for the third time and I feel like giving up.", "response": "That's a genuinely disheartening feeling — three attempts takes real courage each time, even when it doesn't feel that way right now. Failing something publicly and repeatedly, especially something everyone else seems to do easily, can make you doubt yourself in ways that aren't fair to who you actually are. You're allowed to be frustrated and sit with that for a bit before deciding anything about what's next. Whenever you're ready, we can look at what tripped you up this time — sometimes it's one or two fixable habits, not a lack of ability. But right now, it's okay to just feel disappointed."}
{"prompt": "My cat passed away this morning and I don't really know who to talk to.", "response": "I'm so sorry — losing a cat you've shared your home and days with is a real loss, and it's okay that it hurts this much. Grief for a pet doesn't need justifying to anyone, including yourself; the relationship was real, so the loss is real. If it helps to talk about them right now, I'm here — what were they like? If you'd rather just sit with the quiet for a while, that's okay too. Whatever you do today, be gentle with yourself. You don't have to be productive or composed. This is allowed to just be a hard day."}
{"prompt": "I got passed over for a promotion I really wanted and I'm trying not to spiral.", "response": "That's a real disappointment, and it makes sense you'd feel it hard — you cared about this, which is exactly why it stings. Trying not to spiral is its own kind of effort, so credit yourself for noticing the pull and naming it instead of just getting swept into it. This one result doesn't have to become a verdict on your whole trajectory or worth, even though it might feel that way tonight. When you're ready — no rush — we can look at what feedback you got and whether there's a path forward. For now, it's fair to just be upset about something you wanted."}
</tool_response>

{"prompt": "I keep procrastinating on a big project at work and now I'm stressed about the deadline.", "response": "That spiral is so familiar — the project feels big, so you put it off, then the clock starts ticking harder, and suddenly the weight doubles. First, breathe: you are not the first person to be here and you will not be the last. The deadline is real, but so is your capacity to make meaningful progress even starting from a messy place. Try this right now: set a timer for twenty minutes and work on literally the smallest next step. One email, one paragraph, one spreadsheet cell. You don't need to finish anything; you just need to prove to yourself that starting is possible. Often the momentum takes over from there. And afterward, whatever happens, be kind to yourself — this lesson will help next time, and that matters too."}
EOF

I miss them and I don't know what to do.", "response": "What you're feeling is completely normal, and it takes real courage to name that miss instead of pretending you're fine with the distance. This shift you're noticing is often a teenager testing the waters of independence, not a reflection of how much they love or need you. They're learning to live in their own headspace, and that's a healthy step — even when it leaves you wondering where you fit in now. You might try low-pressure invitations: leaving a snack on their desk with a note, asking if they want company for a movie on the couch without expecting a yes, or sharing something small from your day just to keep the thread alive. It's also okay to tell them gently, \"I miss our chats\" — most teens are more receptive to that honesty than they get credit for. The love hasn't gone anywhere; the shape of it is just changing."}
EOF

Panic attacks are your body's alarm system misfiring, not a personal failure or weakness. They can happen to anyone, in any place, and the grocery store is actually one of the more common spots because of the sensory overload: bright lights, noise, crowds, endless choices. The good news is you survived it, and now you have data about what might help next time. Some people find it helps to go during quieter hours, bring headphones, or bring a friend along until the space feels safe again. Deep, slow breathing as you walk through the doors can ground your nervous system. Be patient with yourself — every time you go back, even if it's hard, you're gently teaching your body that the store is safe. You're already braver than you give yourself credit for."}
EOF
</parameter>
